# The master's research thesis

::: {.page-lead}
The thesis is an individual research project supervised by a scientific team. Students formulate a question, choose appropriate methods and critically assess their findings.
:::

::: {.split-section}
::: {}
## Research experience

How can an observation become a testable hypothesis? Which data are needed, and what conclusions do they support? The thesis provides an opportunity to address these questions in practice.

Students contribute to a project, compare their findings with published research and present their work to other scientists.
:::
::: {.note-panel}
### A supervised project

Work starts in the second semester of the first year and continues during the first semester of the second year, with support from a host laboratory and a supervisory team.
:::
:::

## From defining a question to presenting results

::: {.timeline}
::: {.timeline-step}
### Define a research question

Discuss research possibilities with the teams and use your interests to inform the choice of topic.
:::
::: {.timeline-step}
### Develop the study

Read, observe, experiment and analyse, using methods suited to the research question.
:::
::: {.timeline-step}
### Present the findings

The written thesis and oral presentation develop your ability to explain results, recognise limitations and defend your interpretation.
:::
:::

## Research themes {#exemples}

BOE theses address biological and environmental questions at scales ranging from molecules to landscapes. The following themes illustrate the range of research; they are not a list of current thesis openings.

::: {.topic-grid}
::: {.topic-card #ecosystemes}
### Biodiversity and ecosystem functioning

How do species coexist? What makes communities resistant to disturbance? Research examines connections between biodiversity, ecological interactions and ecosystem functioning, including responses to climate change.

**Approaches:** controlled experiments, community analysis and ecological modelling.
:::
::: {.topic-card #organismes}
### Responses to environmental change

Heat, pollution and limited resources impose multiple constraints. Research links behavioural and physiological responses with genetic and epigenetic mechanisms involved in adaptation.

**Approaches:** ecotoxicology, ecophysiology, molecular biology and genomics.
:::
::: {.topic-card #conservation}
### Behaviour, movement and conservation

Feeding, habitat choice and movement are essential aspects of animal life. Understanding behaviour and population dynamics helps assess landscape change and inform biodiversity conservation.

**Approaches:** field observations, movement tracking, mapping and quantitative analysis.
:::
::: {.topic-card #plantes}
### Plants and species interactions

Plant reproduction, stress responses and relationships with other organisms provide a range of research questions. Insect–bacterial associations also help explain how interactions evolve and shape ecology.

**Approaches:** greenhouse and laboratory experiments, field monitoring and molecular methods.
:::
:::

## Choosing a research approach

A thesis may combine field observations, laboratory experiments and data analysis. Discussions with research teams help students develop a project suited to their interests and learn new methods.

Research also develops project management, teamwork, communication and evidence-based argument: skills relevant to a range of careers.
